text: The main deduction pattern here is coverage of reasoning in Analysis (issue 3) and coverage of issues for the procedural points.

The judgment relies on two independent, dispositive grounds: (1) the merits (28-year default), and (2) that the State Commission could not grant final relief via an interlocutory order and the second decisive issue is absent from the Issues list.
Missing costs order in the Conclusion
The follow-on citations (Khushi Ram, Ripudaman Singh) are omitted- but not critical since they are corroborative.

This is a remand order with several distinct directions the rubric specifically flags (remand, qualifications, directions): (1) the High Court is given liberty to frame additional substantial questions of law, not just the three noted; (2) the restored appeals are to be listed before the roster Bench on a specific date (27th August 2024), with parties obligated to appear without fresh notice; (3) interim relief operative as of the impugned judgment is expressly continued; (4) pending applications, including an impleadment application, are disposed of. None of these appear in the Conclusion.

"Filmistan appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave" is a party-role reversal. The High Court ruled in Filmistan's favor (upheld res judicata, blocked the trial from proceeding). The judgment's costs order "Filmistan will pay the costs of the appeal" confirms Filmistan lost this SC appeal, meaning Filmistan was the respondent, not the appellant.
Major S.S. Khanna v. Brig. F.J. Dillon, (1952) 1 SCR 722" is a wrong citation. This case is a 1964 Supreme Court decision (AIR 1964 SC 497), not 1952.
Costs order and issue-rectification direction omitted
A prior revision against the trial court's refusal to try issues 11–13 as preliminary issues was dismissed in limine by the High Court omitted from the FIRAC

It states "Section 5(4) is declared void" but omits that the Court also voided "the procedure prescribed by the impugned Act" affecting those proceeded against under it, and omits the costs award ("petitioner will have his costs"). Two pieces are missing from the actual relief.
Conclusion is appeals allowed not appeal allowed
Important precedents including Commissioner of Police v. Gordhandas Bhanji, Opto Circuits (India) Ltd. v. Axis Bank missed.
Conclusion is appeals allowed not appeal allowed
1966 Act
The statute is identified as "Delhi Administration Act, 1966." This is a fabricated/invented citation.
Cited- Delhi Administration Act, 1966 has no plausible connection to this fact pattern and is not supported anywhere in the source text.
The statute is identified as "Delhi Administration Act, 1966." This is a fabricated/invented citation.

The judgment explicitly treats the High Court's factual misconception about who filed CRR No. 2327 of 2018 as a distinct, self-evidently prejudicial error and a separate ground for interference. This is a decisive issue the Court actually relied on, and it is completely absent from the Issues list.

Issue 3 (whether the HC erred in holding the Sessions Judge "sat in appeal") is listed in Issues but not analyzed at all. Additionally, the factual-misconception ground (para 16, the "second error") which the judgment treats as an independent basis for reversal has no corresponding reasoning chain anywhere in Analysis.

The Court issued two dispositions, not one.he Court also invoked Article 142 to set aside the 9 Sept 2021 order and revive CRR 2327/2018 on the HC's file which is a second, distinct disposition. The FIRAC only implies this via "directed the High Court to decide the pending revisional application," without stating it as an actual order made.
Conclusion is Appeals allowed not appeal allowed
Conclusion omits the judgment's explicit "no release" clarification and the conditional-reconsideration direction

The judgment text itself gives no SCC citation numbers for any precedent, it only names the cases. The FIRAC nonetheless supplies specific citations (e.g., D.J. Bahadur as "(1984) 3 SCC 109," Ram Lal Wadhwa as "(1983) 2 SCC 635," Roshan Lal Tandon as "(1980) 1 SCC 1," Pitchumani as "(1979) 4 SCC 1").
Omits several authorities the Court actually engages with substantively: Mohammad Shujat Ali v. Union of India and British Paints (India) Ltd. v. Workmen
Omits a distinct, material reasoning step: the Court's specific rebuttal to Srivastava's argument that he shouldn't lose his Class III retirement benefit merely because he was promoted
Conclusion doesn't cover all important point.

Omits Respondent No. 1's own case theory: his argument that the Resolution Professional violated SEBI disclosure regulations, that he wasn't a party to the Section 7 proceedings and lacked access to documents, and that this constituted "sufficient cause" for delay.

The judgment builds its "Section 4 doesn't apply to the condonable period" holding through an extended chain of precedents which are Assam Urban, then explicitly reaffirmed in Sagufa Ahmed, Bhimashankar Sahakari, and My Preferred Transformation & Hospitality (all quoted at length). Only Assam Urban is captured; the other three load-bearing authorities in that chain are missing.
Omits two things from the operative order: (1) "there is no order as to costs", and (2) "connected Miscellaneous Application(s)... shall stand closed,"

The judgment cites Ramana Dayaram Shetty together with two other precedents in the same "See" citation — Natural Resources Allocation, In Re (2012) 10 SCC 1 and Manohar Lal Sharma v. Principal Secretary (2014) 9 SCC 516, all three supporting the same "maximum value of state resources" principle. Only one of the three is captured; the other two are dropped entirely

13 appellant-cited precedents (Wasif Haider, Kailash Gour, Sunil Kundu, Karan Singh, Dayal Singh, Shahid Khan, Vijaybhai Patel, Noor Aga on merits; Hem Chand, Manjit Singh, Bavo, Ramnaresh, Yogendra, Gurmukh Singh on sentencing) are cited and rejected by the Court but entirely missing from the FIRAC — including Noor Aga, which is named in the Analysis but never listed as an authority.
Conclusion is Appeals allowed not appeal allowed

The judgment's operative order includes an explicit, specific direction that is omitted: "the recruitment which is now to be re-done by completing the interview examination should be finalised within four months hence."

Analysis omits a procedural nuance: the Supreme Court explicitly states it is not persuaded by the Single Judge's own reasoning   even while reaching the same result, meaning the Court affirmed the outcome via a different, narrower rationale than either lower court used.

In analysis Sundarji Shivji v. Secretary of State for India is labeled "Distinguished." But the judgment does not merely distinguish it on facts, rather it expressly states "we hold that this case had not been correctly decided," actively disapproving its legal reasoning on burden of proof. Also Kalyani Prasad Singh v. Borrea Coal Co. Ltd. is omitted
Kalyani Prasad Singh vs Borrea Coal Co. Ltd. and Bank of Bombay vs Fazulbhoy Ebrahim on burden of proof missed out.

It states "Appeal dismissed" / simplified label "dismissed." The actual result is Appeal allowed, order set aside, no order as to costs.
It states "Appeal dismissed" / simplified label "dismissed." The actual result is Appeal allowed, order set aside, no order as to costs.
It omits that this was a multi-judge, split-opinion case entirely.

FIRAC didn't point out that judges disagreed and reached opposite conclusions on these very issues (e.g., Hidayatullah held sub-delegation invalid; Bachawat held it valid, two majority judges reasoning differently on the same point).
Delegatus non potest delegare principle is presented as resolved in one direction, when in fact it was contested among the majority judges themselves

The Analysis doesn't just omit the majority reasoning, it states a conclusion contradicted by the actual binding holding.

This is a fundamentally broken FIRAC: it appears to have been generated from only one dissenting judgment in a multi-opinion judgment and reports the losing side's reasoning as the Court's holding, with an inverted final outcome.
5-Judge Bench: Analysis should reflect Majority opinion
5-Judge Bench: Analysis should reflect Majority opinion
Appeal is allowed, not dismissed.

Two of the two minority opinions in Mary Cheriyan (Govindan Nair, J. and Krishnamoorthy Iyer, J., with distinct reasoning) collapsed into one undifferentiated "minority"; the ~10-case string of concurrent-findings precedents (Srinivas Ram Kumar, Addagada Raghavamma, etc.) entirely omitted.

Missing the Court's rebuttal of the co-ownership argument (para 45, based on the two deceased donees' heirs never inheriting); and missing the Court's express prospective-only application of its ruling.
Beyond the missing costs order ("No costs") and the missing "Trial Court to proceed further as per law" direction, the Conclusion omits the prospective-application qualification entirely.

The FIRAC supplies precise citations — "AIR 1965 SC 963" for H.C. Goel, "AIR 1952 SC 354" for Abdul Majid, "[1930] A.C. 333" for Raphael v. Brandy, "[1934] A.C. 176" for Reilly v. The Queen, "AIR 1960 SC 100" for State of Tripura, none of which are traceable to the source.
Omits two authorities the judgment discusses substantively as part of the same contract-vs-status debate: Inland Revenue Commissioners v. Hambrook and Terrell v. Secretary of State for the Colonies.
Omits the costs disposition entirely: the judgment specifies "dismissed with costs to the respondent, Baishankar Avalram Joshi.
Section 220(4) hallucinated in place of Section 220(3)

Omits the recurring "interlocutory applications disposed of" line, and more materially, drops half the HC's affirmed direction:  reporting only "no permanent construction" while omitting "waterbed and structures kept clean and maintained."
Omits Textile Labour Association v. Ahmedabad Millowner's Association, a case the appellants themselves cite and which the Court actively distinguished.
Omits the judgment's explicit costs order.

The FIRAC cites Aswini Kumar Ghosh v. Arabinda Bose as "AIR 1952 SC 369" and Dominion of India v. Shrinbai A. Irani as "AIR 1952 SC 213." although the source judgment's own footnotes for these citations are garbled/incomplete.

The Analysis states: "This reduction resulted in the extinguishment of the rights attached to the 15,32,41,012 shares that were cancelled." This specific figure is both arithmetically wrong and not stated anywhere in the judgment.
hallucination in cancellation figure - 15,32,41,012

Accurate as cited, but presents "consent cannot confer jurisdiction" and the Rule 31 scope principle as the Court's settled view, when these were specifically Pathak J.'s reasoning for the position that did not prevail in the final order.
Chinnappa Reddy J.'s entire reasoning, the fitment-anomaly argument, and his direct rebuttal of Pathak J. — is completely absent.
Court's actual holding is given wrong
Issue 1 is reasonably framed but implicitly assumes there's a single, unified answer when in fact the two judges gave opposite answers to it.

Conclusion states both appeals are dismissed "upholding the original award and the Tribunal's order dated 22 December 1978" i.e., the corrigendum stands. This is actually consistent with the true outcome, but it directly contradicts the FIRAC's own Analysis section, which just concluded the corrigendum was invalid and should be quashed. A reader following the document from Analysis to Conclusion encounters two incompatible holdings on the same question.
